entities.span: As the operator, I want a per account and app wide budget on outside job search calls,
rejected_spans: so a bug or a burst of interest cannot run past the source's terms or run up cost I would pay myself.

entities.span: As a signed in user, I want a plain reason when a search is blocked,
rejected_spans: so I know it is a budget limit rather than something broken.

entities.span: As the operator, I want the failure alert proven to fire for real,
rejected_spans: so a total, silent denial cannot happen here the way it did on the project this one learns from.

entities.span: **AC-1**: A `job_search` call attempt is decided by one atomic database function that checks three windows together in the same call: the caller's own weekly count, the app wide daily count, and the app wide monthly count. Proven atomic under concurrent calls against a real database connection, not a mock.

**AC-2**: An attempt that would put any one of the three windows over its cap is refused, and refusing consumes no budget in any of the three windows. The attempt is still counted (see AC-9) in every window it was checked against, whether it was allowed or refused.

**AC-3**: A refusal names one reason from a closed set (`account_week_cap_reached`, `global_day_cap_reached`, `global_month_cap_reached`). When more than one window is over at once, the reason names the caller's own window before either app wide window,
rejected_spans: because that is the one the person can act on themselves.

entities.span: **AC-4**: An engaged kill switch refuses the call before the atomic window check ever runs, reading `readKillSwitch()` (feature 3) directly rather than a second reader of `app_settings`. It reports one of two reasons, never collapsed into one: `kill_switch_engaged` when the read succeeded and the switch reads on, `kill_switch_unavailable` when the read itself failed. Both fail the call closed; only the reason differs,
rejected_spans: because a deliberate flip and a broken read must never look identical to the person on the other end, the same distinction spec 0002 already protects for the switch's own dashboard rendering.

entities.span: **AC-5**: A refusal, for any of the five reasons (AC-3's three plus AC-4's two), is never reported through `failure()`. It is a successful decision whose answer is no: `success({ allowed: false, reason })`. A refusal that were reported as a failure would mark the gate's own span failed every time the system works exactly as designed, corrupting the one ratio AC-10's alert depends on.

**AC-6**: An unrecognised `call_type`, or a `call_type` missing any one of its three required `usage_cap` rows (account/week, global/day, global/month; partial configuration is treated the same as none), is reported through `failure()` with a new `FailureKind` member, `usage_gate_misconfigured`, severity `unexpected`. The atomic function never raises to signal this: it returns `configured: boolean` as an ordinary output column. `configured: false` is what `checkUsageGate()` maps to this failure; the `allowed`/`reason` columns carry no meaning when `configured` is false.
rejected_spans: since a Postgres exception surfaced through `.rpc()` arrives at the Supabase client as `{ data: null, error }`, not a thrown exception, and would otherwise pass straight through `attempt()` as an unparsed success, the same trap `readKillSwitch()`'s own comments document.

entities.span: **AC-7**: The named span for the whole gate operation, `usage_gate.check`, opens as the first statement, before the kill switch pre-check and before anything else, including the `getClaims()` identity check in AC-13.
rejected_spans: A kill switch left engaged, a broken kill switch read, or the gate function itself failing outright, is a total denial, and a span opened later would leave that exact failure with no denominator.

entities.span: **AC-8**: Trace sampling is 1.0 on `usage_gate.check` in production (already provided by the existing `NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE` configuration from spec 0002).

**AC-9**: Every call for a **configured** `call_type` that reaches the atomic gate function increments an attempt counter inside that same function, unconditionally, regardless of the decision. An unconfigured `call_type` increments no counter at all (AC-6). Visibility into a misconfiguration does not depend on the write: `usage_gate_misconfigured` reaches Sentry as its own `unexpected` severity failure regardless of whether a counter row exists.
rejected_spans: so a hammered and blocked window is distinguishable from a quiet one purely from the stored counters, independent of Sentry.

entities.span: an earlier version of this criterion read "every call," full stop, which let any authenticated caller create and grow `usage_gate_counter` rows without bound simply by varying `call_type`,
rejected_spans: since the counter write ran before the configuration check.

entities.span: **AC-10**: Two failure rate alert rules, both written down in `docs/observability/` and configured in Sentry. Configured 2026-09-03 in the one `jobhunt` Sentry project (org `ghalys-org`) as four metric monitors: the two rules times the `development` and `production` environments, two environment-scoped copies of each rule in a single project — there is no separate Sentry project per environment; spec 0002 index line 79 records the setup as "an organisation and a project", and environments are separated by the `environment` tag. Each monitor is dataset `Spans`, visualize `failure_rate()`, interval `1 day`, High priority Above `0.2`, Medium Above `0.19`, Resolve default, and each has an alert connected that notifies `mghalynho@gmail.com` on all four issue triggers. Sentry's Threshold form has no attempt floor: Threshold is a bare value on the metric with no minimum sample count anywhere in the form (verified in the form on 2026-09-03), so a lone failure in a quiet 24 hour window reads as 100%, and the 1 day interval is the partial mitigation. A follow-up below considers an absolute count threshold instead, which would give a natural floor at this app's volume. Sentry also requires two priority thresholds where this spec defines one: Medium is pinned at 0.19, just under High's 0.2, so the two fire together rather than expressing a second alerting policy no document describes (recorded 2026-09-03). Revisit the numbers if traffic ever grows enough to change that assumption. The alert query filters by failure kind (carried in the `failure.kind` span attribute `failure()` sets), not "any failed span": the `usage_gate.check` monitors filter `span.description:usage_gate.check` and `failure.kind is not session_missing`, which keeps the intended numerator — `usage_gate_misconfigured`, `database_unavailable`, and `external_service_failed` (the `getClaims()` call can throw, e.g. a JWKS outage, wrapped with this kind; corrected 2026-09-03, a fresh model review found this third kind unnamed here), the unexpected kinds this span can carry. The `kill_switch.read` monitors filter `span.description:kill_switch.read` only, their numerator its own existing, unchanged failure kinds. The attribute exists specifically because the span's status message, which `failure()` also sets, is not a queryable field in Sentry: verified 2026-09-02 against a real forced failure, a failed span carries `span.status: internal_error` in the dashboard and nothing naming which kind failed, so a rule cannot filter by kind against the status alone. A metric monitor detects but does not notify: creating one creates no alert, and the Connected Alerts list stays empty until an alert is attached by hand — the first firing on 2026-09-03 produced a Critical issue with nothing delivered, which is why AC-11's smoke test must confirm the connection and `docs/reflexes.md` now carries the standing rule.
rejected_spans: since a kill switch outage and a gate outage are different failures with different spans (see the Key invariants note on `kill_switch.read`'s own span)

The design wanted a ratio with an absolute attempt floor — at the global monthly ceiling of 2,000 calls this app averages under 3 calls an hour, so a floor reachable inside a single hour would only ever cross during an actively searching session, staying silent on an ordinary quiet day exactly when a real misconfiguration would too — but

because AC-5's five refusal reasons are successes that never mark the span failed in the first place, and `session_missing` is the one expected failure excluded by name (a caller with an expired token is not evidence the gate is broken).
All three unexpected kinds belong in the numerator deliberately: each is a total denial of the gate for a reason that is not the caller's own usage, the exact failure AC-10's ratio exists to catch.

entities.span: **AC-11**: A forced failure smoke test, run locally against the development Supabase project and the `development` environment of the one `jobhunt` Sentry project, never the `production` environment of that same project and never a Vercel Preview deployment, proves the whole chain: the span records a failure, sampling captures it, the fingerprint groups it, the threshold is crossed, an alert is connected to the monitor, and a real alert is delivered. The connected alert half is load bearing: a metric monitor detects but does not notify, and the first firing on 2026-09-03 produced a Critical issue, correctly assigned, with nothing delivered because the monitor's Connected Alerts list was empty. The temporary call this test adds must load `/profile`, never `/health`: Sentry's project level inbound filter "Filter out health check transactions" discards `/health`'s entire transaction, and every span nested inside it, at ingest, while error events raised on the same request are unaffected by that filter and arrive normally. A smoke test run against `/health` therefore shows the error event landing while `usage_gate.check` never appears, which reads as a broken span when nothing is wrong with it.
rejected_spans: (Preview samples at 0.1, so roughly nine in ten forced failures there would never be captured, per `docs/observability/README.md`)
— exactly the failure this criterion exists to catch, and one a paper review of the alert rule passes every time (recorded in `docs/experiments/0011-usage-gating-and-kill-switch.md`)

entities.span: **AC-12**: The three cap values (25 per account per week, 66 app wide per day, 2000 app wide per month, for `job_search`) live in a database configuration table editable with no deploy, not as a literal in code, matching the kill switch's own no deploy operating model.

**AC-13**: The account scope is keyed on a session verified with `getClaims()`, matching the pattern already used everywhere else in this codebase (`proxy.ts`, `(app)/layout.tsx`, `profile/queries.ts`, `profile/actions.ts`), never `getSession()`, which reads the cookie's contents without verifying them against the auth server, and never a raw, unverified cookie read of any other kind. A forged session on this path spends someone else's budget, not just reads someone else's data.

**AC-14**: A database failure while reading the cap configuration or writing the counters fails closed: the call is refused, matching the project's named risk rule and the kill switch's own existing fail closed default. `checkUsageGate()` inspects the `.rpc()` response's own `error` field before reading `configured`, `allowed`, or `reason`: a non null `error` maps to `database_unavailable`, and `data: null` with no `error` is itself also treated as `database_unavailable` rather than as an absent decision. This matters beyond AC-6's misconfigured case: a genuine database fault (a statement timeout, a lock timeout, a revoked grant, a dropped table) arrives through the same `{ data: null, error }` channel as an ordinary refusal, not as a thrown exception, so `attempt()` catches nothing and code that reads only the output columns would see `data: null` and make no decision at all, which is a silent open, not a fail closed one.
**AC-15**: Both new tables (`usage_cap`, `usage_gate_counter`) have row level security enabled and forced, matching every existing table in the schema, even though neither carries a policy yet.
